notes:
Task and constraints: Apply replacement operations at original string indices when each source substring matches.
Idea: Mark valid replacements in a bucket by start index, then scan the original string once to build the result.
Technique and why it applies: Each valid operation stores source length and target characters. During output construction, a replacement appends its target and skips the source length; otherwise one original character is copied.
Invariant: bucket[i] stores the replacement beginning at original index i, if its source matched.
Edge cases: The match check verifies source characters remain within S. Multiple operations at one index would overwrite each other in the bucket, but the problem guarantees distinct indices.
Complexity: Checking sources costs O(total source characters), and building output is O(n+target output length); bucket storage is O(n).

Task and constraints: Return the sum of distances from every tree node to all other nodes.
Idea: Root the tree at zero, use postorder to compute subtree sizes and subtree distance sums, then preorder to reroot those sums.
Technique and why it applies: For a child c, distances from the parent shift by +1 for nodes outside c's subtree and -1 for nodes inside. The formula updates each child's total in constant time after subtree data is known.
Invariant: tree_nodes[u] is the size of u's subtree, and distances[u] is the sum of distances from u to nodes in that subtree before rerooting.
Edge cases: n is assumed positive and the input is a tree. Recursive DFS can exceed Python's recursion limit for a very deep tree.
Complexity: Each edge is traversed twice, giving O(n) time and O(n) graph/array/recursion space.

Task and constraints: Compute the distance sum for every node of a tree.
Idea: Run one DFS to compute subtree sizes and root distance totals, then a second DFS to transfer totals to children.
Technique and why it applies: result[child] equals result[parent]-count[child]+(N-count[child]); distances to subtree nodes decrease by one, while distances to outside nodes increase by one.
Invariant: count[u] stores subtree size and result[u] stores the sum of distances from u to all nodes after the reroot step reaches u.
Edge cases: The tree is assumed connected and nonempty. Recursion depth can reach O(N) on a path-shaped tree.
Complexity: Both DFS passes are O(N) time, and adjacency lists plus arrays use O(N) space.

Task and constraints: Find the maximum overlap between two binary images when one is shifted over the other.
Idea: Record coordinates of all ones and count the frequency of every relative translation between a one in each image.
Technique and why it applies: If two one-cells align under shift (dx,dy), they contribute one overlapping cell. The most frequent offset gives the largest overlap.
Invariant: shiftDict[(dx,dy)] is the number of one-cell pairs aligned by that translation.
Edge cases: If either image has no ones, shiftDict stays empty and the method returns zero. defaultdict is used without importing it, so it requires an external import.
Complexity: With a and b one-cells in the images, time is O(ab) and space is O(ab) distinct offsets.

Task and constraints: Compute the largest number of overlapping ones between two binary images under translation.
Idea: Enumerate every one-cell pair and increment a counter indexed by their relative row and column displacement.
Technique and why it applies: A translation aligns exactly the pairs with the same displacement. The maximum count over all displacement buckets is the best overlap.
Invariant: count[shift] stores the number of aligned one-cell pairs for that shift.
Edge cases: All-zero images leave count as zeros, so max returns zero. The images are assumed square and equal-sized.
Complexity: Every pair of cells is considered, giving O(n^4) time and O(n²) displacement storage.

Task and constraints: Determine whether two axis-aligned rectangles overlap with positive area.
Idea: Reject any pair separated horizontally or vertically; otherwise they overlap.
Technique and why it applies: If one rectangle's right edge is at or before the other's left edge, or one top edge is at or below the other's bottom edge, their interiors do not intersect.
Invariant: The condition checks all four possible separating directions.
Edge cases: Touching edges or corners are not considered overlap because comparisons use inclusive separation checks. Rectangles are represented by [x1,y1,x2,y2].
Complexity: A fixed number of comparisons gives O(1) time and O(1) space.

Task and constraints: Check whether two rectangles have a nonempty intersection of positive width and height.
Idea: Test overlap independently on the x and y axes.
Technique and why it applies: The projections intersect only when max(left endpoints) is strictly less than min(right endpoints). Both axes must intersect for the rectangles to overlap in area.
Invariant: intersect reports whether the intervals on one axis overlap with positive length.
Edge cases: Strict inequality rejects rectangles that only touch along an edge or at a corner.
Complexity: The checks use O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Calculate the probability that the score in the New 21 Game is at most n, drawing points until the score reaches k.
Idea: Use a sliding window over terminal probabilities for scores from k through k+maxPts-1, then work backward.
Technique and why it applies: Every score below k transitions uniformly to the next maxPts possible scores, so its probability is the average of those successor probabilities. The deque and running sum maintain this window average.
Invariant: s is the sum of the current deque of successor probabilities, and dp[0] after each step is the probability from the newly prepended score.
Edge cases: The code uses collections.deque without importing collections, so it requires an external import. k=0 would make the setup return an unintended state; normal constraints handle that case separately or constrain inputs.
Complexity: The sliding window takes O(k+maxPts) time and O(maxPts) space.

Task and constraints: Simulate dominoes falling left or right until all forces settle.
Idea: Propagate directional pushes in rounds, accumulating signed force at cells reached from neighboring fallen dominoes.
Technique and why it applies: L contributes -1 to its left neighbor and R contributes +1 to its right. A cell receiving opposing forces in the same round has net zero and remains upright; nonzero cells continue propagation.
Invariant: arr records net force at each cell, and d tracks positions already reached so they are not processed repeatedly.
Edge cases: Initially fallen L/R cells are marked before propagation. A cell reached by equal opposing forces remains zero and becomes '.' in the output.
Complexity: Each cell is activated at most once, giving O(n) time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Return the final domino configuration after simultaneous pushes from the left and right.
Idea: Compute rightward force in a left-to-right pass and leftward force in a right-to-left pass.
Technique and why it applies: Forces decay by one per empty cell and reset at opposing dominoes. Their signed difference determines whether a cell falls right, left, or stays upright.
Invariant: force[i] is the accumulated rightward force minus leftward force at position i.
Edge cases: Existing L and R reset the opposite force. Equal forces cancel to zero, preserving '.'.
Complexity: Two scans take O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count connected groups of strings where any two strings are similar if they differ in at most two positions.
Idea: Treat strings as graph nodes and use DFS to find connected components under the similarity relation.
Technique and why it applies: isSimilar compares each pair position by position. DFS visits every string reachable from a starting string, and each new unvisited start adds one group.
Invariant: visited contains strings already assigned to a component.
Edge cases: The method uses diff_count<=2 rather than requiring exactly zero or two differences; this is valid under the problem's anagram constraint, where one mismatch cannot occur. Duplicate strings are similar.
Complexity: Pairwise comparisons cost O(N²L) for N strings of length L, and visited/recursion space is O(N).

Task and constraints: Count 3-by-3 magic squares inside a grid.
Idea: Check every 3-by-3 window for equal row sums, equal column sums, equal diagonal sums, and nine distinct values beginning at one.
Technique and why it applies: A 3-by-3 magic square has each row, column, and diagonal summing to 15, and contains exactly the integers 1 through 9. The helper checks sums and uniqueness.
Invariant: nums stores values seen in the current window; sum_diag and sum_anti accumulate its two diagonals.
Edge cases: The code checks only that the minimum value is one and there are nine distinct values, not explicitly that the maximum is nine; equal sums and nine distinct positive grid values usually constrain this strongly, but it is not a direct range check.
Complexity: Each window takes constant work, so time is O(RC) and auxiliary space O(1).

Task and constraints: Determine whether all rooms can be visited starting from room zero using keys found in rooms.
Idea: Use BFS from room zero, adding keys found in each newly visited room to a queue.
Technique and why it applies: A key creates a directed edge to another room. BFS explores every room reachable from zero; if the visited count equals the total room count, all rooms are accessible.
Invariant: visited_rooms contains rooms already processed, and queue holds discovered room indices.
Edge cases: The code uses collections.deque without importing collections in the snippet, so it needs that name externally. Keys may enqueue duplicates, which are skipped when popped.
Complexity: Each room is processed once and each key is scanned once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V) queue/visited space.

Task and constraints: Check whether every room is reachable from room zero through keys found in rooms.
Idea: Run iterative DFS with a stack and a set of discovered rooms.
Technique and why it applies: Each key points to a room reachable from the current room. Newly discovered rooms are added to lookup and pushed onto the stack; reaching all rooms returns True early.
Invariant: lookup contains every room discovered so far.
Edge cases: Room zero is initially marked. If no keys lead to some room, the final size comparison returns False.
Complexity: Each room and key is processed once, giving O(V+E) time and O(V) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Split a digit string into a Fibonacci-like sequence of integers with each value within the signed 32-bit limit.
Idea: Try every legal first and second number, then recursively consume the rest by requiring each next number to equal the previous two's sum.
Technique and why it applies: A Fibonacci sequence is determined by its first two values. consume_tail checks whether the decimal representation of their sum is the next prefix and recurses on the suffix.
Invariant: current contains a valid prefix sequence whose adjacent last values determine the next required number.
Edge cases: Leading-zero multi-digit numbers are rejected. MAX is set to 2**31, not 2**31-1, so values equal to 2^31 can be incorrectly accepted despite the signed 32-bit limit.
Complexity: The two starting-number loops and recursive matching can be exponential in string length in the worst case, with O(n) recursion/list space.

Task and constraints: Find a Fibonacci-like sequence represented by the entire digit string, respecting the 32-bit signed integer bound.
Idea: Try possible first and second numbers, then repeatedly parse the exact next sum from the remaining string.
Technique and why it applies: The next value is forced by the previous two. startswith accumulates digits until it matches that sum or exceeds it; success continues until the whole string is consumed.
Invariant: fib is a valid sequence prefix and k is the next unconsumed string position.
Edge cases: Leading zeros are allowed only for the single digit zero. The bound MAX_INT is 2^31-1 and is checked before adding adjacent values.
Complexity: The search over starting lengths is O(n²) candidates with repeated scans, giving O(n³) worst-case time and O(n) space.

Task and constraints: Compare two strings after interpreting # as backspace.
Idea: Iterate each string backward, skipping deleted characters with a debt counter, and compare surviving characters from the end.
Technique and why it applies: A # increases debt, and each preceding ordinary character consumes one unit of debt before it can be yielded. zip_longest compares streams of surviving characters.
Invariant: Each generator yields exactly the characters that remain after backspaces, in reverse order.
Edge cases: The code uses zip_longest without importing it, so it needs that name externally. Different surviving lengths compare unequal because zip_longest supplies a fill value.
Complexity: Each character is visited once, giving O(n+m) time and O(1) auxiliary space beyond generator state.

Task and constraints: Determine whether S and T are equal after backspace operations.
Idea: Generate surviving characters backward while tracking how many prior characters each # deletes.
Technique and why it applies: findNextChar skips a character when skip is positive; otherwise it yields that character. zip_longest detects both differing characters and unequal surviving lengths.
Invariant: Each generator yields the final string in reverse order.
Edge cases: Empty strings yield no characters and compare equal. The code uses O(1) extra state per generator.
Complexity: The two scans take O(n+m) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find the longest mountain: a strictly increasing run followed by a strictly decreasing run, both nonempty.
Idea: Compute increasing-run lengths ending at each index and decreasing-run lengths starting there.
Technique and why it applies: A peak is valid only when both lengths exceed one. Combining them as up+down-1 counts the peak once.
Invariant: max_up[i] is the increasing run ending at i, and max_down[i] is the decreasing run starting at i.
Edge cases: Arrays shorter than three return zero. Equal adjacent values break both strict runs.
Complexity: Two passes take O(n) time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest strict mountain subarray.
Idea: Track the current increasing and decreasing run lengths while scanning adjacent pairs.
Technique and why it applies: An increase after a descent or an equality resets both phases. A mountain exists once both up_len and down_len are positive; their sum plus one gives its length.
Invariant: up_len counts rising edges in the current candidate mountain and down_len counts falling edges after its peak.
Edge cases: Strict comparisons ensure equal values cannot belong to a mountain. Arrays without both phases return zero.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
